themes.name: other: unexpected_charge
themes.problem_statement: Statements about unexpected charge that fit no specific theme.
themes.root_cause: unassigned or low-confidence rows

themes.name: Overdraft fee charged when the money was already there
themes.problem_statement: An overdraft or NSF fee is charged even though a deposit, transfer or payment had already posted or was visible as pending, often triggering further cascading fees.
themes.root_cause: Overdraft fees are assessed on posting order and settlement timing rather than the balance the customer can see, so fees land before an available deposit is recognized.
examples: A $67.00 overdraft fee was taken out of the account once the $1,100.00 check cleared.
The balance was brought to the bank's own stated -$50.00 no-fee threshold before the new day, but an overdraft fee was still charged, triggering three more cascading fees totaling $130.00.

themes.name: Fee refund refused because a reversal quota is used up
themes.problem_statement: The customer asks for overdraft or service fees to be reversed and is refused because an annual or per-period cap on reversals has already been reached, even when the bank caused the fee.
themes.root_cause: A fixed cap on fee reversals per customer per period is applied regardless of whether the fee came from bank error or hardship, so valid requests are declined by rule.
examples: Multiple overdraft fees were charged on the same day the account first went negative, and Chase refused to reverse them beyond the one reversal allowed per year.
Thirteen overdraft fees totaling $440.00 were charged in one month, but representatives said a yearly reversal quota had already been met and only reversed $66.00 of the total.

themes.name: Monthly fee charged although the waiver terms were met
themes.problem_statement: A monthly maintenance fee is charged even though the account met the published waiver criteria, such as a qualifying deposit, minimum balance or linked account, and refunds require chasing.
themes.root_cause: The fee engine does not correctly detect qualifying activity such as automatic transfers, balances or linked accounts before assessing the monthly charge.
examples: Chase charged a $5.00 monthly fee for three months straight, claiming no auto-deposit was set up, even though a $25.00 automatic transfer to savings runs with every direct deposit.

Monthly service fees of $12.00 or $8.00 were sporadically charged despite meeting the waiver requirements, and after reaching the annual refund limit, the customer had to visit a branch each time to get refunded.

themes.name: A settled charge is taken again or reversed twice
themes.problem_statement: A charge, refund or credit that was already processed or confirmed is taken or reversed a second time with no new authorization, pushing the account negative and generating fees.
themes.root_cause: Reconciliation and dispute handling re-apply or re-reverse transactions without checking them against the account's current settled balance and history.
examples: The double charge caused a negative account balance and excessive fees, an issue the customer says has happened before.
Taking back the disputed refund pushed the account into overdraft, generating numerous fees from the bank's own reversal.

themes.name: Fees still taken from a frozen or legally held account
themes.problem_statement: Fees and debits keep coming out of an account that is frozen, locked or under a garnishment or estate hold, with no advance notice, and refunds are refused for months.
themes.root_cause: Holds and freezes stop customer access but do not suspend automatic fee assessment and debits, and staff do not disclose these charges when the hold is applied.
examples: Chase has taken unexplained charges from the locked account and a local branch told the customer to leave without releasing the Social Security check.
Despite prepaying the safe deposit box fees a month early, Chase debited the frozen estate savings account by more than $400.00 again, and the branch manager has denied refunding it for months.

themes.name: Repeat overdraft fees charged before balance can be fixed
themes.problem_statement: Several overdraft fees are charged in quick succession as transactions and retries post against a negative balance, with no chance to add funds first.
themes.root_cause: Each transaction or retry posting against a negative balance triggers its own fee, with no pause, daily cap or grace window before further fees are assessed.
examples: Multiple $34.00 overdraft fees were stacked rapidly for small debit transactions under $10.00, and Chase denied a full reversal, citing policy without addressing the stacking.
$780.00 in overdraft fees on small-dollar ACH and card payments were charged in rapid succession without a meaningful opportunity to cure, worsening the account balance.

themes.name: Fees still charged after the account was closed
themes.problem_statement: Fees, interest or automatic withdrawals keep hitting an account the customer already closed or asked to close, sometimes reopening a settled balance.
themes.root_cause: Closure requests do not reach the billing, fee and payment systems, so scheduled fees, interest accrual and merchant autopay keep running on the closed account.
examples: After bringing a new account to a zero balance to close it, a fee was charged instead of the account being closed.
The company withdrew $160.00 through autopay from the bank account after the account was closed and before the bill even arrived, leaving no chance to review or dispute the charge.

themes.name: Bank does not undo every fee caused by its own error
themes.problem_statement: A charge, fee or interest caused by a bank processing mistake (wrong account, wrong amount, mistaken retry) stays on the account even after the bank confirms the error.
themes.root_cause: Correction teams reverse only the item the customer reports, leaving the customer to find each knock-on fee instead of unwinding the whole error once it is confirmed.
examples: Late fees and courtesy fees totaling nearly $300.00 piled up while waiting for the refund checks to be corrected and reissued.
The manager set up the wire from the customer's personal account instead of his fee-free business account, resulting in an unexpected wire fee.

themes.name: Ordinary purchase billed as cash advance or foreign use
themes.problem_statement: A normal purchase is coded as a cash advance or a foreign transaction, adding a fee and interest that starts immediately, with no warning at the time of the sale.
themes.root_cause: The transaction coding used to price fees does not match what the customer actually bought, and the resulting classification is never disclosed before the purchase.
examples: A 3% fee was charged for using a debit card at a merchant, though debit card purchases should not carry that fee.
A $92.00 charity purchase was charged a $10.00 cash-like transaction fee and coded as a cash advance subject to nearly 30% daily interest, with no way to pay off just that portion.

themes.name: New fee or changed term applied without advance notice
themes.problem_statement: The customer is charged a new or changed fee, interest or penalty after a limit, rate, due date or promotional term changed without anyone telling them beforehand.
themes.root_cause: Changes to fee-relevant terms take effect in billing before a reliable advance-notice step reaches the customer, and promises made by staff are not recorded against billing.
examples: A $34.00 interest charge was applied because $530.00 of the statement balance was paid one day after the minimum due date, even though it was paid two days before the statement cycle closed.
A $750.00 balance transfer fee was charged the cycle after the loan opened, despite the statement noting it was a promotional offer.

themes.name: Subscription billed without consent or after cancelling
themes.problem_statement: The customer is billed month after month for a membership they never knowingly agreed to, or that keeps charging after they cancelled and the merchant confirmed it.
themes.root_cause: Recurring merchant charges are authorised against the stored card without checking consent, and a reported cancellation does not block later attempts by the same merchant.
examples: The customer was charged $210.00 per month for two years, totaling $4600.00, for a membership they never agreed to after only signing up for one month of sessions.

A duplicate membership was unknowingly billed $16.00 per month for about 36 months with no usage or benefit, and the merchant refused to refund beyond a limited internal policy threshold despite confirming no usage.

themes.name: Autopay ignores the customer's start or stop request
themes.problem_statement: Autopay fails to run, is not switched off when asked, or restarts on its own, causing late fees, overdrafts and payments the customer never authorised.
themes.root_cause: Autopay enrolment, cancellation and suspension requests taken by service staff are not reliably synced to the payment system that actually moves the money.
examples: Chase's autopay system rejected a payment and later failed to turn on again after being told it was fixed, resulting in multiple late fees, one of which Chase refused to refund.
The customer never enrolled in autopay and explicitly asked Chase to stop all automatic payments, but unauthorized charges kept being processed, pushing the balance over $2000.00.

themes.name: Insurance forced onto mortgage despite existing cover
themes.problem_statement: The customer is charged for lender-placed hazard or flood insurance although their own policy was in force, often costing more while covering less than it.
themes.root_cause: Insurance tracking flags a lapse and force-places a policy without matching the proof of continuous coverage already on file, leaving the customer to re-prove it.
examples: Chase purchased a flood insurance policy costing double the homeowner policy while covering less than the prior policy and its own appraisal value, weeks after ignoring the customer's emailed concerns.
Chase required expensive lender-placed insurance and would not release the Declaration page needed to get cheaper outside insurance.

themes.name: other: money_held_or_not_returned
themes.problem_statement: Statements about money held or not returned that fit no specific theme.
themes.root_cause: unassigned or low-confidence rows

themes.name: Deposit held over a phone check the customer cannot pass
themes.problem_statement: A check or third-party deposit stays restricted because the issuer's or endorser's phone number must match, and the hold continues even when a working number is supplied.
themes.root_cause: Verification may rely on a single phone-based check of the check writer with no fallback, so an outdated or unreachable number blocks release despite other proof.
examples: A remaining account balance has been held for 15 months because Chase's phone verification requirement for the third party does not match the customer's documented situation, despite substantial evidence supporting the c
The account was restricted after depositing an inheritance check that the fiance, who lacks valid ID, endorsed over to the customer, and Chase would not lift it without verifying his phone number.

themes.name: Funds stay held after the deposit is confirmed legitimate
themes.problem_statement: A deposit or transfer is confirmed as cleared or legitimate by the sending bank, another department or the customer's own proof, yet the funds stay held indefinitely.
themes.root_cause: Verification queues may have no step that closes the case and releases funds once outside confirmation arrives, and no time limit governs how long a hold may run.
examples: The account was frozen after depositing tenants' rent checks over suspected fraud, and even after Chase called the tenant and confirmed the checks were legitimate, the bank still kept the check.
Chase locked the account for unusual activity but still accepted two job direct deposits, and is now withholding that earned money without a clear reason.

themes.name: Promised refund or closing-balance check never arrives
themes.problem_statement: After an account closes, funds are held, or a refund is approved, a check is promised by a set date and then arrives far later or never, despite repeated follow-up.
themes.root_cause: The back office that issues and mails refund and closing-balance checks may have no tracking or service level, so a promised check can be lost or never generated.
examples: Chase closed the checking account to investigate an alert and has kept about $1,600.00 with no timeline for when it will be refunded.

After publicly criticizing Chase and filing a CFPB complaint, the customer's checking account was restricted then closed and a $1,100.00 balance remains inaccessible, and a credit card account was separately closed citin

themes.name: ATM cash deposit not credited, or the credit reversed
themes.problem_statement: Cash deposited at an ATM is swallowed, under-credited or errors out with no receipt, and any provisional credit issued for the shortage is later taken back unresolved.
themes.root_cause: ATM faults during cash deposits may not be reconciled against the machine's own cash count, so investigations default to reversing the credit instead of settling the shortage.
examples: An ATM deposit of $9,500 in cash was credited only $8,500, and a $1,000 provisional credit issued for the shortage was later reversed.
An ATM deposit of $2,200.00 in cash intended for rent errored out, reset, and never issued a receipt, and the cash was never credited to the account.

themes.name: Account closed or frozen, cutting off access to the money
themes.problem_statement: An account is closed, frozen or restricted with little or no advance notice, and the customer loses access to their money with no reason given and no release date.
themes.root_cause: Closure and risk-restriction actions may execute immediately on a trigger with no paired notice or funds-release step, so access is cut first and explained later, if at all.
examples: After reporting fraud with a police report, the checking account was frozen and has remained inaccessible for years, with Chase refusing to close it or restore access.
The account was closed for inactivity the day after a $3000.00 check deposit, and the funds were mistakenly processed toward the closed account.

themes.name: Confirmed transfer or refund vanishes and cannot be traced
themes.problem_statement: A transfer, bill payment or merchant refund confirmed as sent never appears in the account, and the bank's own records cannot say where the money ended up.
themes.root_cause: Transfer, bill-pay and refund records may not be reconciled across systems, so a confirmed movement that fails to post leaves no audit trail to follow or reverse.
examples: A $600.00 transfer from an external credit union account never appeared in the checking account despite a notice that it would be available.
A rejected wire transfer was never explained or returned despite repeated follow-up, threatening a home purchase closing and already damaging the customer's credit score.

themes.name: Provisional dispute credit taken back without a reason
themes.problem_statement: A temporary credit is issued for a disputed charge or fraud claim and then reversed before the investigation finishes, or without any evidence-based reason given.
themes.root_cause: Dispute cases may be closed or overridden before the required review period ends, with no documented proof needed before the provisional credit is clawed back.
examples: After crediting back $750.00 for three fraudulent $250.00 transactions, Chase removed the credit again, leaving the account overdrawn despite assurances of reimbursement.
A dispute over merchandise that was never delivered had its temporary credit recouped by letter, leaving the checking account overdrawn by $210.00.

themes.name: Deposit held far longer than promised or usual
themes.problem_statement: A check or deposit is held well beyond the standard, promised or previously experienced availability period, with shifting timelines and no clear reason for the delay.
themes.root_cause: Hold durations may be extended or reset with no service-level limit or escalation path, so a routine hold can run on instead of clearing within the disclosed period.
examples: A $590.00 payroll check deposited at the ATM was held despite usually being available, forcing her to borrow money to pay bills and avoid late fees.
A $2,000.00 employer paycheck deposit, consistent with her regular deposits, was held for 13 days under automatic fraud prevention despite a clean account history, and a manual review was refused.

themes.name: Legal hold or court order applied too broadly to funds
themes.problem_statement: Funds are frozen or garnished under a legal hold, levy or court order that withholds more than was ordered, targets the wrong person, or is not lifted after a release.
themes.root_cause: Legal-process handling may execute orders without verifying their scope, matching identity to the named party, or confirming a release before funds are unblocked.
examples: A court order instructed Chase to remit $250.00 to the plaintiff's counsel and release the remaining balance to the customer, but Chase instead transferred the entire balance to the garnishing party.
The account was frozen based on a legal hold from a court order that reportedly does not contain the customer's correct legal name, with no documentation provided.

themes.name: Incoming deposit taken to cover a disputed debt
themes.problem_statement: An incoming check or benefit payment is applied against a claimed or disputed debt instead of being credited to the customer, with no proper notice or consent.
themes.root_cause: Deposits to accounts with an outstanding balance may run through an automatic offset that requires no notice, no check of the debt's validity, and no customer consent.
examples: After the account was closed, Chase applied two disability checks sent to it in error toward a claimed debt without giving proper notice.
Chase applied the customer's Social Security check to an $840.00 balance created by fraudulent checks it knew were unauthorized, and won't transfer the money to the new account.

themes.name: Deposit sent to the wrong account is not returned
themes.problem_statement: A payment, refund or deposit goes in error to an account that is not the customer's, and the bank will not freeze, reverse or return the funds even after prompt notice.
themes.root_cause: Recall requests may not be actioned before settlement and are not honored afterwards without a formal recall from the originating bank, leaving the funds where they landed.
examples: After banking info was changed without authorization, $5,300.00 in backpay and a $2,500.00 paycheck were sent to a Chase account that is not the customer's.
A $3700.00 direct deposit was sent to a stranger's account due to a data entry error, and Chase refused to freeze or reverse it despite immediate notification.

themes.name: Required provisional credit for fraud is never issued
themes.problem_statement: After an unauthorized transaction is reported, the provisional credit required within the Regulation E deadline is never issued and the amount stays uncredited and unexplained.
themes.root_cause: Fraud-dispute intake may not be tied to a tracked Regulation E clock, so a claim can pass the provisional-credit window with no automatic escalation or credit issued.
examples: Chase has not issued the required provisional credit for a $1,000.00 unauthorized withdrawal well beyond the Regulation E business-day deadline, with no written explanation despite multiple follow-up attempts.

Over 30 days after Chase identified and reported the fraud, no provisional credit has been issued as required under Regulation E, leaving the account negative and her liable for a stolen down payment.

themes.name: Payment misdirected to wrong or unintended account, unrecove
themes.problem_statement: A check, wire, or payment is confirmed sent to or deposited into a Chase account that does not belong to the intended recipient (wrong account number, wrong branch action, or data-entry error), and Ch
themes.root_cause: Misdirected-item recovery is not automated or prioritized once a payment posts to the wrong account; without a recall from the sender, staff have no standard path to reverse or disclose the receiving
examples: A $3,700 deposit was confirmed by the branch and the sending bank to have gone into another customer's account, but Chase offered no way to correct it.
Investment checks for over $110,000.00, made out to the customer and their brother, were deposited into a Chase account that is not theirs instead of the intended investment house.

themes.name: Rewards points lost when the account is closed
themes.problem_statement: A card account is closed or cancelled and the accumulated or just-earned rewards points are immediately forfeited or blocked from redemption, with no advance notice.
themes.root_cause: Closure processing may revoke the linked rewards balance at once rather than opening a redemption window, and staff apply forfeiture even where program rules would not.
examples: Unable to resolve the points issue in time, the customer ended up paying out of pocket for flights for his wife and daughter to join the trip.

After being encouraged by Chase to open a checking account for a promotion, the credit cards used to earn points for the same promotional push were closed for 'too many accounts,' forfeiting the earned points.

themes.name: Payment sent to a known wrong recipient is not recovered
themes.problem_statement: A Zelle, wire or ACH payment reaches an identifiable wrong recipient - a mistyped number, a stale contact, a name mismatch - and the bank says it cannot get the money back.
themes.root_cause: These payment rails may treat an accepted payment as final with no compelled-return mechanism, so once funds post the bank can only ask the receiving party to send them back.
examples: A $33000.00 wire was confirmed received by the recipient despite his claim otherwise, but the receiving bank cannot recall the funds without his permission, which he refuses to give.
Chase accepted a wire transfer into an account that doesn't allow incoming wires but never applied the funds or sent them back, despite more than a week of calls.

themes.name: other: no_response_or_follow_up
themes.problem_statement: Statements about no response or follow up that fit no specific theme.
themes.root_cause: unassigned or low-confidence rows

themes.name: Promised callback or follow-up never happens
themes.problem_statement: A banker, branch manager or department commits to calling back, sending an update or completing an action by a set time, and nothing happens unless the customer chases it.
themes.root_cause: Verbal callback commitments may never be logged or assigned an owner in any system, so nothing forces the promised contact to actually take place.
examples: A branch teller submitted an earlier payment incorrectly causing it to be declined, and complaints about it plus promised escalation callbacks were never returned.
An unrecognized $6000.00 withdrawal was initially denied by phone, and after filing a claim with a police report as instructed, the claims department never got back in touch.

themes.name: Requested or promised document is never sent
themes.problem_statement: A document the customer needs or was told would arrive - a title, lien release, notice, invoice, letter or written confirmation - never comes, and paperwork sent in is not acknowledged.
themes.root_cause: Document generation and intake may run on manual, unlogged steps with no confirmation or tracking, so a request can be dropped without anyone noticing.
examples: Chase never sent any notice that a co-signed auto loan was past due, in collections, or charged off, and the customer only learned of it when their security clearance was put at risk.
Refund checks from cancelling extended warranty and tire protection were sent directly to the customer, and nobody told them the money had to go to Chase.

themes.name: Claim investigation runs past its deadline with no status
themes.problem_statement: A claim or investigation runs weeks or months past the promised timeframe, and repeated calls return only a generic 'still reviewing' with no status, reason or next step.
themes.root_cause: Investigations have no enforced service-level clock and no status visible to agents, so frontline staff can only repeat a holding message instead of giving a real update.
examples: The protection company did not provide a clear or justified response despite being asked to explain the denial and provide supporting documents.
After multiple calls and reaching the escalation team, the customer was repeatedly told there was no update and no timeline for when the funds would be deposited.

themes.name: Promised refund, credit or bonus is never actually paid
themes.problem_statement: The bank confirms a refund, provisional credit, bonus or check will be issued, but it never arrives even though the customer met every requirement and followed up repeatedly.
themes.root_cause: Approval and disbursement sit with different teams and share no tracking, so an agreed payout never triggers the payment and nobody notices it was missed.
examples: A Chase representative said he processed a refund of 3 late fees and return-payment fees, but it was never done and there is no record of it.
A branch employee showed on his screen that the $200.00 savings bonus requirements were met and promised a follow-up email, but the bonus was never applied and no follow-up ever came.

themes.name: Departments pass the case around and nobody owns it
themes.problem_statement: A case stalls because branch, back office, fraud and legal teams each say another department owns it, will not talk to each other, or block the customer from reaching the team that can act.
themes.root_cause: Cases needing action from more than one team have no single named owner or cross-team escalation path, so each department can hand the customer on without resolving anything.
examples: Chase branches say the invoicing service is a separate company they cannot assist with, while the processor only accepts support tickets and has no phone number, leaving the customer with no clear path to resolution.

Closing deceased parents' joint accounts and disbursing the funds has stalled for over two months after all documents were submitted, with the branch, back office and legal department passing the case around.

themes.name: Documents already submitted are lost and requested again
themes.problem_statement: The customer sends the same proof or paperwork several times because the bank reports it as never received or not on file, delaying the claim by weeks or months each time.
themes.root_cause: Documents arriving by fax, mail or branch are not reliably logged against the case file, so every new handler treats earlier submissions as missing and asks for them again.
examples: Chase keeps asking for documentation already submitted, delaying repayment for over two months and causing the elderly customer significant distress.
Faxed proof of the actual debtor's bankruptcy filing and a written withdrawal of the restraining notice from the creditor's attorney were repeatedly reported as not received by Chase.

themes.name: Executive office or assigned contact stops responding
themes.problem_statement: After escalating to the executive office, a compliance team or a named contact, the customer gets no reply at all to calls, emails or certified letters about their case.
themes.root_cause: Escalation channels have no backup coverage or duty to close the loop, so once a case is assigned there it can sit unanswered with nobody tracking whether a reply went out.
examples: An email and certified letter sent to Chase's executive office asking for reinstatement and an explanation went unanswered.
A complaint filed with Chase's Executive Office received no written response.

themes.name: Written requests go unanswered and are redirected to phone
themes.problem_statement: The customer submits a request in writing and asks for a written reply, but never receives one; the bank only tells them to call instead, so the request is never acted on.
themes.root_cause: Letters and secure messages are not routed into a tracked queue that must produce a written reply, so agents default to telling the customer to call.
examples: Multiple written requests for hardship program enrollment went without a direct response, and Chase repeatedly redirected the customer to call despite a stated preference for written communication.

themes.name: Calls continue after a formal do-not-call request
themes.problem_statement: The customer formally asks for contact to stop by do-not-call request or cease-and-desist letter, but collections and other calls keep arriving, sometimes several times a day.
themes.root_cause: Do-not-contact requests are not reliably flagged on the account or passed to the outbound dialing and collections systems, so scheduled contact attempts carry on.
examples: Despite mailed and emailed cease and desist requests on two chase accounts, chase continues calling three times a day plus emails and written communication.
Despite explicitly asking to be placed on the do-not-call list, another collections call came in, prompting the customer to record it and threaten to report the incident.

themes.name: other: long_wait_or_delay
themes.problem_statement: Statements about long wait or delay that fit no specific theme.
themes.root_cause: unassigned or low-confidence rows

themes.name: Mortgage assumption stalls on repeated document requests
themes.problem_statement: A mortgage assumption after a divorce, court order or partner buyout sits in underwriting for months or over a year as the same or new documents are requested after each submission.
themes.root_cause: Assumption underwriting may have no checklist fixed up front, so each reviewer re-requests items already supplied and the review clock restarts instead of tracking elapsed time.
examples: A loan assumption to buy out a business partner has been pending for over 3 months without a decision, threatening a 1031 exchange deadline.

A mortgage assumption application from a divorce settlement has been repeatedly delayed past the original 90-180 day timeline and the 30-day regulatory notice requirement, with the decision date pushed back from 30 to 45

themes.name: Hours on hold and repeated transfers without reaching help
themes.problem_statement: Customers spend hours on hold, are transferred between departments and call centres, or are disconnected before anyone takes on the issue they called about.
themes.root_cause: Call routing may pass customers through multiple queues with no single owner for the issue, and there is no callback or hold-time safeguard to catch disconnects.
examples: Since the restriction, the customer has spent days being put on hold for an hour or more, transferred, promised callbacks, and disconnected with no resolution, and now wants to close the account entirely.
After being told Chase would call back in 3 business days, the customer had to call again after 10 days, was put on hold for 30 minutes, and got hung up on.

themes.name: Card benefit claim stuck under review for months
themes.problem_statement: A travel delay, trip cancellation or purchase-protection claim on a card benefit stays under review for months after the customer has submitted complete documentation.
themes.root_cause: Third-party claims administrators handling card benefits may have no enforced turnaround time, and re-request documents already provided instead of deciding the claim.
examples: A trip cancellation claim filed for a card benefit has been open for nearly 4 months, with the third-party claims administrator repeatedly requesting the same documentation already provided.
A trip delay claim on the Chase Sapphire Reserve has been stuck in 'pending adjuster review' for over four months despite repeated confirmations that all documents were complete.

themes.name: Dispute runs past the legal resolution deadline
themes.problem_statement: A fraud or billing dispute investigation runs well past the 90-day or other regulatory window, often with no written explanation of the delay or of the outcome.
themes.root_cause: Dispute queues may not be monitored against Regulation E and Z deadlines, so a case can pass the limit without forcing a resolution or the required consumer notice.
examples: A $2,100.00 fraud claim was denied for months before Chase finally returned the money, and the customer never received the legally required written explanation for the initial denial.
Chase has delayed resolving the unauthorized-withdrawal dispute and has not confirmed provisional credit was issued within Regulation E timelines.

themes.name: Refund or payment posts long after the promised date
themes.problem_statement: A refund for an overpayment, or a routine card payment, posts days or weeks after the timeframe the bank itself promised, leaving the customer without their money.
themes.root_cause: Refund and payment posting for these cases may depend on manual back-office steps with no service level enforced against the processing time that was disclosed.
examples: An accidental credit card overpayment refund, first promised as a mailed check and then as a return to checking, has not arrived after many business days, exceeding the required 7-day window.
An accidental overpayment to a Chase credit card was promised back within 14 business days, but daily calls since then have not resolved the missing money.

themes.name: other: incorrect_or_conflicting_information
themes.problem_statement: Statements about incorrect or conflicting information that fit no specific theme.
themes.root_cause: unassigned or low-confidence rows

themes.name: Different reps give contradictory answers on one case
themes.problem_statement: Staff, branches and departments tell the customer different things about the same case - a title's status, a hold, a closure reason, whether a check was mailed - with no consistent answer.
themes.root_cause: Case notes and status may not live in one shared system every representative can see, so each person reconstructs the story from memory or a partial record.
examples: Three different Chase supervisors gave three different, contradictory stories about whether the paid-off vehicle's title was mailed, released electronically, sent elsewhere, or never received.
A manager flatly denied a prior representative's authority and the existence of notes and calls that were confirmed as recorded by Chase itself.

themes.name: Staff assurance reversed by a later back-office decision
themes.problem_statement: A representative confirms an outcome - a bonus qualifies, a coupon applies, a payment is deferred, a claim is approved - and the bank later reverses it.
themes.root_cause: Frontline staff may confirm outcomes without checking the authoritative system of record or the fine print, so a back-office review applying different criteria overrides them.
examples: A 'Just For You' pre-screening offer implied pre-approval for an auto loan, but the application was denied after applying.

After Chase initially agreed a $340.00 lease charge was invalid and returned the funds through the customer's bank, it later reinstated the balance despite a stop payment on file, and a rep admitted choosing to pursue th

themes.name: Dispute denied for a reason unrelated to the charge
themes.problem_statement: A fraud or billing dispute is denied, or a credit reversed, on reasoning - another purchase, an unrelated transfer, an automated rule - that does not match the transaction in question.
themes.root_cause: Dispute reviewers may close cases with a generic rule or automated match instead of checking the specific transaction and the evidence the customer submitted.
examples: An $800.00 unauthorized Apple Pay charge's temporary credit was reversed because the customer had made other authorized transfers to their daughter, not because this specific charge was found authorized.
A customer service agent confirmed the claims department relied on an algorithm to deny the claim and never issued a provisional credit.

themes.name: Check confirmed as good is later bounced or held anyway
themes.problem_statement: The customer is told a check or deposit is verified, authorized or cleared, and it is then returned, held, or used to restrict the account despite that earlier confirmation.
themes.root_cause: Verification and hold decisions happen separately at teller, phone and back-office stages, with no record of the earlier confirmation carried forward to the later one.
examples: Chase threatened to close the account because the settlement check could not be verified due to a mismatched phone number, until the lawyer provided a secondary number.
A deposited check that already cleared is being held up because Chase says the verification number provided is not associated, even though it was given as instructed.

themes.name: Fee, interest or policy terms never disclosed up front
themes.problem_statement: A fee-triggering rule, an interest-calculation method or a required disclosure is never explained at signing, and the customer only learns of it after being charged.
themes.root_cause: Fee and interest mechanics may appear only in fine print at origination, with no step where someone walks the customer through the terms that will actually cost them money.
examples: Chase never provided written instructions to keep making payments while the GAP claim was pending or warned that not doing so could result in a charge-off.
A representative confirmed interest accrues daily at 8.64% regardless of payment timing, a method never disclosed at signing, causing interest charges to swing wildly on a supposedly fixed-rate loan.

themes.name: Bank states a checkable fact that turns out to be false
themes.problem_statement: The customer or a regulator is told a specific, verifiable fact - a call was made, a check was fraudulent, funds were returned, a deposit never arrived - that proves untrue.
themes.root_cause: Staff and case handlers may state facts from assumption or an incomplete record rather than verifying them against the counterparty or the transaction history first.
examples: Over more than a month and roughly twenty calls, representatives repeatedly promised the $3000.00 would arrive, only for the customer to learn the check had been returned to the issuer weeks earlier.
The accounts were closed with no explanation, and a fraud notice arrived well after the fact, backdated to before the closure.

themes.name: Money shown as available is pulled back with no reason
themes.problem_statement: A deposit, credit or balance shows as available and confirmed, then is reduced, reversed or withheld later with no new information to explain the change.
themes.root_cause: Provisional postings may be shown to the customer before back-office verification finishes, and the reversal is not paired with a concrete, disclosed reason.
examples: An ATM deposit of $1,900.00 was recorded as only $930.00 after investigation, leaving the customer owing $960.00 and overdrawn.
A $400.00 deposit displayed as available balance was later deemed unavailable, causing the account to go negative and multiple overdraft fees to be charged.

themes.name: Requirements to resolve a case keep expanding
themes.problem_statement: Every time the customer meets a stated requirement to release funds or close a case, a new one appears that was never mentioned, and no complete list is ever given up front.
themes.root_cause: Cases may be handled ad hoc by whichever representative picks them up next, each adding a condition, instead of one documented checklist agreed at intake.
examples: After her mother passed away, Chase froze the joint account and, over multiple branch visits and weeks, kept changing what paperwork was required to close it, discovering along the way that the account had never actually
Representatives are rude on calls and keep inventing new excuses, most recently claiming they must investigate an unrelated prior deposit, to justify withholding the money.

themes.name: Charged-off debt still reported and collected on
themes.problem_statement: An account already written off as a loss keeps being reported to credit bureaus as owed and pursued through settlement offers and collection contact.
themes.root_cause: Charge-off status recorded internally may not propagate to the systems that furnish credit-bureau data and drive collection outreach, so both continue unchanged.
examples: A charged-off debt is still being reported and collected on, which the customer says the IRS confirmed is illegal without issuing the corresponding 1099-C.
An account charged off by Chase, which should be a completed tax write-off, still shows as a debt owed on his credit report, and Chase continues sending settlement notices to collect on it.

themes.name: Payments applied to the wrong balance on the account
themes.problem_statement: Payments, refunds or credits land on a promotional 0% balance or an unrelated plan instead of the intended or highest-interest balance, and statements do not show where they went.
themes.root_cause: Payment allocation logic may not follow the agreed or required order, such as highest-APR first, and statements do not expose which balance a payment actually reduced.
examples: Large payments on several statements were applied partly or wholly to a 0% interest balance transfer instead of the balance charged 20.24% interest, despite disputes.
Chase has been misapplying payments toward the $14000.00 0% balance transfer instead of regular purchases, resulting in interest being charged on the purchases.

themes.name: Unauthorized accounts or inquiries appear on credit report
themes.problem_statement: An account, inquiry or debt the customer never opened or consented to appears on their credit report or is pursued by a collector, with no prior notice or chance to dispute.
themes.root_cause: Furnishers and collectors may post tradelines, inquiries and collection accounts without verifying consent or identity, and skip any pre-reporting notice window.
examples: Inquiries that I never gave written consent for are appearing on my consumer report and shouldn't be visible.
An unfamiliar credit card account was reported on the credit profile without prior notice, dropping the credit score.

themes.name: Disputed credit-report entry is never properly checked
themes.problem_statement: A disputed balance, status, date or charge-off stays uncorrected or reappears after a formal dispute, with no documentation of how the investigation was actually carried out.
themes.root_cause: Disputes may be closed with a generic verified-as-accurate reply rather than by producing underlying records, and corrections do not propagate across all bureaus.
examples: Removing the fraudulent inquiry required a different, harder process at one bureau, and even a confirmed removal from one bureau still appeared on its own report.
Chase reported incorrect information related to the fraud dispute on the customer's credit reports, causing tens of thousands of dollars in extra costs.

themes.name: Application denied on facts the documents disprove
themes.problem_statement: A credit, loan-assistance or assumption application is denied citing a credit score, a delinquency or a financial profile that the customer's own submitted paperwork contradicts.
themes.root_cause: Decisions may be made from an automated screen reading a stale or partial record, with submitted documents never pulled into the review before the denial reason is issued.
examples: A HELOC application was denied for a credit score below the minimum threshold, even though Chase's own mobile app and other sources show a higher score above that minimum.
A mortgage assistance application was denied based on delinquency alone, without Chase ever reviewing the submitted updated SSDI income and household support documentation.

themes.name: Unrecognized entries on statements, no records provided
themes.problem_statement: Statements, payment histories or credit reports show transactions, balances or delinquencies the customer never made, and requests for check copies or source documents go unmet.
themes.root_cause: Servicing records carried across transfers and internal systems may never be reconciled to source documents, and there is no process for producing that evidence on request.
examples: The loan statement lists payments the customer never made, shows two misapplication entries for the same amount on the same days, and an escrow advance not explained in any paperwork received.
Unexplained principal payments appear on the loan account that don't match any extra payments actually made, and copies of the underlying checks have not been provided.

themes.name: other: denied_or_declined_without_explanation

themes.name: Account closed and the bank will not say why

themes.root_cause: Closure decisions come from an automated back-office risk process that front-line staff and supervisors cannot see into, so no one is able to disclose the real reason.
examples: The customer received a notice that the accounts would close within 10 business days with no reason provided, threatening the ability to pay past-due rent.
Chase closed the account without an official reason, offering only vague explanations like too many aggressive withdrawals or reversals, which even the agents called unfair.

themes.name: Funds held because a third party's phone cannot be verified
themes.problem_statement: A deposit or transfer stays blocked because a co-depositor, endorser or check issuer's phone number cannot be verified, and ID, pay stubs or other proof are refused.
themes.root_cause: Third-party identity checks for deposits rely only on matching a phone number in an internal database, with no fallback for a legitimate person who cannot be matched that way.
examples: Despite providing IDs, pay stubs, and proof of joint account ownership, the funds remained blocked because the co-depositor's phone number could not be verified.

An IRS refund check endorsed by the customer's husband, deposited with prior bank approval, led to the account being restricted and closed because his phone number couldn't be verified, and Chase won't accept his ID or p

themes.name: Fraud dispute denied without reviewing the evidence
themes.problem_statement: A fraud or transaction dispute is denied, or a temporary credit reversed, without reviewing camera footage, device logs or merchant confirmation that contradicts the decision.
themes.root_cause: Investigators close cases on a narrow automated check, such as matching card and PIN use or an IP address, instead of pulling and weighing the evidence actually available.
examples: A $1200.00 charge that Chase's own fraud department initially flagged after multiple suspicious attempts was later denied for lack of documentation, even after the merchant confirmed the fraud and a refund.
After two weeks, Chase said it could not prove fraud and required the customer to prove they didn't make the charges and to contact the merchant's fraud department directly.

themes.name: No payment relief for a car that cannot be driven
themes.problem_statement: A borrower whose vehicle is unusable from a defect, recall or documented disability gets no payment hold, deferment or schedule change while payments keep coming due.
themes.root_cause: Hardship and deferment requests are judged on standard underwriting criteria only, with no path for a vehicle that is out of service through no fault of the borrower.
examples: A car is non-functional due to a known manufacturer software issue with no service being offered, and Chase, the loan holder, has been asked to hold the loan payment but has not accommodated this.

Despite an active year-long recall and repeated safety defects making the leased vehicle unsafe and unable to generate income, Chase Auto has not delayed the payment schedule to reflect its inoperability.

themes.name: Account or loan application denied with no reason given
themes.problem_statement: An application is denied, or returns a generic error, even though the customer meets the stated requirements, has a long-standing relationship or supplied full documentation.
themes.root_cause: Screening applies internal risk-scoring rules that are not disclosed to front-line staff, so denials cannot be explained even when the visible profile appears to qualify.
examples: A $50,000.00 auto loan application was denied citing insufficient income, vehicle value, credit inquiries, and a past bankruptcy, reasons the customer believes are insufficient and discriminatory.
A long-time customer with hundreds of thousands of dollars running through Chase business accounts has been denied an auto loan multiple times with no explanation.

themes.name: Promised account-opening bonus never paid
themes.problem_statement: The customer meets every stated requirement of balance, deposit and timeframe for an account bonus, but it is never paid, refused over a lost promo code or a technicality.
themes.root_cause: Bonus eligibility tracking and the payout system are not reliably linked, so a validated promotion can silently fail to pay and closures near the payout date go unchecked.

After a first wired deposit was rejected as not qualifying for a $300.00 checking bonus, Chase told the customer his employer payment still wasn't an acceptable 'direct deposit' even after he followed the bank's own guid

themes.name: Account restricted over a check that already cleared
themes.problem_statement: An account is restricted, reversed or closed over a check or deposit that had already cleared or been verified, as if the item were still unconfirmed.
themes.root_cause: Fraud and hold-review triggers run independently of the cleared status recorded elsewhere in the bank's own systems, so a settled item can still set off a restriction.
examples: The bank said it would close the account and send the money back to the check writer even though the check has already cleared.
The account was restricted even though the check deposit that triggered it had already cleared.

themes.name: Fee refund refused for hitting a yearly reversal limit
themes.problem_statement: A request to reverse a fee caused by bank timing or documented hardship is refused because the customer has already used up an annual cap on fee reversals.
themes.root_cause: Fee-reversal approval is gated by an automatic yearly count limit that fires regardless of whether the fee came from a bank processing error or documented hardship.
examples: The requested fee reversal was denied because the customer had reached a limit for fee reversals, despite the fee resulting from automated timing rather than account misuse.

A $100.00 overdraft fee that caused serious financial hardship after job loss cannot be refunded because the customer already had three overdraft fees reversed earlier this year, hitting the yearly limit.

themes.name: Access blocked despite proof of legal authority
themes.problem_statement: The customer supplies trust documents, a power of attorney or a court order proving authority over an account, and the block or restriction stays in place anyway.
themes.root_cause: Legal-authority documents handed to branch or legal staff never reach the team that maintains the hold, so the restriction survives after authority has been proven.
examples: Chase's legal team won't accept trust documents proving full trustee status, and refuses to provide contact information so an attorney can investigate, blocking access to a brother's accounts for months.
Despite a court order fully affirming the power of attorney, the bank continues to block access to about $14000.00 in the dependent adult's account and has not lifted the hold.

themes.name: Estate or legal-authority documents provided but access stil
themes.problem_statement: Customer submits valid legal-authority documentation - a death certificate, power of attorney, certificate of trust, or court judgment - but Chase still refuses to release funds, retitle the account,
themes.root_cause: Legal, estate, and branch teams handle authority documentation inconsistently with no single owner, so validated documents don't reliably translate into the requested account action.
examples: Chase removed the customer as an authorized owner/signatory on personal and business accounts without a court order, valid document, or consent, based on disputed documentation.
Chase is calling the customer's deceased mother's account abandoned and refuses to release the funds even after a death certificate was provided.

themes.name: Fee or overdraft reversal capped by an internal policy limit
themes.problem_statement: Customer asks Chase to reverse overdraft or other fees, but the bank applies a fixed cap on how many can be waived, leaving a balance owed regardless of the circumstances or a cited regulatory violati
themes.root_cause: Fee-waiver tooling enforces a hard per-account or per-year cap on reversals with no override path, even when the customer cites a specific bank error or regulatory violation.
examples: Chase refused to reverse the overdraft fees as bank error despite a Regulation CC violation being cited, instead offering courtesy refunds.
Chase declined to bring the account current excluding all overdraft fees, saying its policy allows removing only three fees, still leaving over $500.00 owed.

themes.name: Power of attorney accepted or revoked without proper checks
themes.problem_statement: A valid power of attorney is declined with no stated reason, or is acted on or revoked without the required verification steps, leaving the account locked or exposed.
themes.root_cause: POA review sits with a legal team that does not consistently apply or communicate its own verification requirements, so decisions are unpredictable and unexplained.
examples: A lawful power of attorney submitted while the mother was hospitalized was declined by Chase legal with no reason given, and the account was then locked.
Chase let an incapacitated trustor revoke the POA and checking account access without waiting for medical documentation, despite having reviewed and frozen the account before.

themes.name: Valid alternative payment method refused at the counter
themes.problem_statement: The customer tries to pay a balance with a legitimate instrument, such as a remittance coupon or a payment flagged only for a name mismatch, it is refused, and late fees accrue.
themes.root_cause: Payment-acceptance rules reject non-standard instruments with no override or escalation path, even when the funds and the payer can be verified.
examples: Chase refused to accept a remittance coupon submitted as payment on the account, and late fees and interest continue to accrue as a result.
The branch refused to accept the payment due to the name issue, with the due date at risk of passing.

themes.name: Hardship payment plan denied with no stated criteria
themes.problem_statement: A customer with documented hardship such as job loss or a fixed income asks for a reduced-payment plan and is refused outright, with no written criteria or reason.
themes.root_cause: Hardship decisions are made against undisclosed internal criteria with no published standard, so a reasonable request can be refused with nothing the customer can act on.
examples: A retiree on a fixed income requested a short-term hardship payment program twice, offering $100 a month for nine months, but was denied both times without written criteria or a reason.

After job loss from an extended maternity leave, every other credit card issuer agreed to a hardship repayment plan except Chase, which continues to deny any option besides paying the full bill to become current.

themes.name: Closed account not reopened though policy allows it
themes.problem_statement: An account closed for inactivity or a no-fault review is eligible for reopening under the bank's own stated policy, but reinstatement requests are refused or passed around.
themes.root_cause: Front-line and reconsideration staff have no reliable way to apply or override the closure policy, so a technically eligible reopening still gets refused.
examples: Despite policy allowing reopening, representatives refused and kept transferring the call, forcing the customer toward a new account that would drop their score even more.
Chase closed the credit card account for inactivity, and Chase's own website says such accounts should be reopenable since there was no other problem like fraud.

themes.name: Required written notice of a decision never arrives
themes.problem_statement: A credit application is denied, a dispute closed or an agreement revoked, and the legally required written notice explaining the decision is never sent.
themes.root_cause: Notice generation runs as a separate step from the decision system, so required adverse-action or dispute-outcome letters are skipped, lost or never triggered.
examples: A recorded call has a Chase supervisor admitting a credit re-evaluation was denied for a past due balance not backed by any policy, and that no Adverse Action Notice was generated.
Applications for a new credit card and a credit limit increase were both denied, and Chase refused to send the correspondence required by law explaining the denial.

themes.name: Legitimate transfer blocked with no way to override
themes.problem_statement: A wire, transfer or payment is blocked or cancelled by a fraud or verification check, and no escalation, override or alternative is offered even with proof it is genuine.
themes.root_cause: Fraud and identity holds are enforced as automatic hard stops, with no manual override or alternate verification route available to front-line staff.
examples: Autopay payments in a balance liquidation program are being rejected by Chase from an externally linked checking account, even though the customer's bank confirms no blocks.
A wire transfer to a cryptocurrency exchange was denied because the customer would not commit in advance to which currency would be purchased, since that depends on market conditions.

themes.name: Payment sent to the wrong recipient is never recovered
themes.problem_statement: A wire or app payment reaches the wrong recipient after a typo or a misclick, and no recall or real investigation is attempted; the loss is called impossible to reverse.
themes.root_cause: Error resolution for wires and P2P payments depends on the receiving bank's voluntary cooperation, with no formal recall process the bank will start on the customer's behalf.
examples: A $10,000.00 wire sent to the wrong account due to a typo has been stuck for a month because Chase refuses to send the hold harmless letter the receiving bank requires, saying it isn't a fraud case.
Despite reporting discrepancies multiple times, the financial institution and the P2P platform said recovering lost funds was impossible and tracking the transactions unfeasible.

themes.name: ATM takes or withholds cash and the account is not fixed
themes.problem_statement: An ATM errors, jams or times out during a cash deposit or withdrawal, so money is taken but not credited or not dispensed, and the shortfall is not corrected promptly.
themes.root_cause: ATM faults are not automatically reconciled against the machine's own cash count, leaving a slow manual investigation that tends to side with the recorded amount.
examples: An ATM took $60.00 in cash bills during a deposit attempt but never credited the amount to the account.
An ATM malfunctioned during a deposit and did not credit the account; a phone rep later credited the claimed amount but it was reversed days later with Chase claiming a smaller amount was deposited.

themes.name: Phone number check blocks a legitimate customer's money
themes.problem_statement: A required phone verification step fails because the number is old, reassigned, foreign or unreachable, and the bank then blocks transfers, access or account closure for the real owner.
themes.root_cause: Identity and transaction verification depends on a single phone-number lookup with no alternative proof accepted, so any mismatch stops the customer completely.
examples: After a banker verified the customer's identity with state paperwork and moved funds to a newly opened account, $110000.00 in wire transfers were rejected again the next day for the same unresolved identity verification

She cannot close her account because she no longer has the US address or phone number used at registration, and neither an in-branch identity check nor updating her contact info let the online system process the closure.

themes.name: Account lock cannot be undone, or keeps coming back
themes.problem_statement: An account is locked for security and the only unlock route is one the customer cannot use, such as a branch visit while overseas or a code to a lost phone, or the lock returns afterwards.
themes.root_cause: The unlock workflow has one hardcoded remediation path with no fallback, and lock state is not synced across channels, so an agent's unlock does not stick.
examples: The account was locked for security and Chase says it can only be unlocked at a branch, but the customer is overseas with no Chase location nearby and can't access funds or pay the Chase credit card.
My Chase mobile app got locked while trying to send a payment, and to unlock it they require a debit card I don't have, with no alternative verification offered.

themes.name: Fraud alerts never reach the customer until money is gone
themes.problem_statement: Unauthorized transactions, new device access or account takeover are not flagged or notified to the customer, who only discovers the losses after they have already happened.
themes.root_cause: Alert rules miss anomalies such as new devices, large transfers and forwarding-rule changes, and there is no second notification channel when the first one fails.
examples: After getting a new card and being placed under a security measure meant to send text alerts for each withdrawal, the customer received no alerts and another $93.00 unauthorized withdrawal occurred.
An unrecognized device the customer never owned has been authorized and accessing the account daily, with no alert ever sent.

themes.name: Known system bug silently breaks an advertised feature
themes.problem_statement: An advertised feature such as autopay migration, a sign-up bonus, a points transfer or account linking fails because of a known internal bug, and the customer is not warned beforehand.
themes.root_cause: Known defects are recorded internally as 'known issues' but never surfaced to customers or fixed on a timeline, so people keep committing money to a feature that does not work.
examples: During the year-end migration from XXXX to Chase Auto, established autopay and payment history did not carry over, and inaccurate migrated data caused another delinquent payment.

A $900.00 account-opening bonus coupon was not enrolled due to a system issue and was only fixed after a customer service call, by which point $15,000.00 had already been deposited assuming it was applied.

themes.name: Card keeps being declined despite available credit
themes.problem_statement: The card is declined for purchase after purchase even though credit or funds are available and identity has already been verified, with no reason given and no lasting fix.
themes.root_cause: The authorization scoring system intermittently blocks valid transactions, and frontline support has no tool to see why or to clear the block permanently.
examples: After the card was locked and replaced due to ongoing fraud, the digital replacement card kept declining for several days despite repeated assurances it had been fixed, disrupting work and appointments.
After each credit card payment, the account displays available credit but the card is declined in stores; this has happened three times and Chase cannot guarantee it will stop.

themes.name: Autopay or scheduled payment fails and causes a late fee
themes.problem_statement: A payment correctly scheduled or enrolled in autopay does not go through because of a system-side error, leaving the customer with a late fee, a credit mark, or a manual payment to make.
themes.root_cause: Autopay linkage, cutoff timing and account-number handling fail intermittently, and the failure is not detected or flagged to the customer before a fee or delinquency is applied.
examples: Losing online access disrupted timely credit card payments normally made through the linked checking account, and a separate payment app was detached from the account without consent.
The autopay set up for the balance transfer did not deduct as scheduled, so the customer had to pay $150.00 manually the next day.

themes.name: System reverts a saved preference or corrected detail
themes.problem_statement: The customer opts out of paperless or marketing email, or corrects their address, and the system silently restores the old value, so the unwanted mail and wrong data come back.
themes.root_cause: Customer-entered preferences and corrections are not held as the source of truth, so a background sync or default process periodically overwrites them with stale data.
examples: Despite receiving confirmation each time that he was unsubscribed from credit card collection emails, he continued receiving them at least ten more times over the following months.
Declining the app's paperless pop-up is repeatedly ignored, and Chase switches the account to paperless anyway despite a stated disability that makes paperless inconvenient.

themes.name: Travel booking fails or changes, causing a missed flight
themes.problem_statement: A flight booked through the bank's travel service is cancelled, mis-booked or never ticketed, and the customer only finds out at the airport or has to rebook elsewhere at their own cost.
themes.root_cause: The travel platform's ticketing integration with airlines is unreliable, with data mismatches, no name validation and booking-engine failures that are not caught before departure.
examples: Flights booked through Chase Travel for a family pilgrimage were cancelled without notice, and a later wrong-class rebooking caused a denied boarding with an infant lacking a ticket number.
Two of the family's round-trip tickets were voided without notice at the airport, forcing a stressful 48-minute call before they were reinstated at the last minute.

themes.name: Transfer sent to the wrong recipient with no check first
themes.problem_statement: A payment, transfer or points redemption goes to the wrong or unauthorized destination because the system never confirms the recipient first, and it cannot be recovered afterwards.
themes.root_cause: Transfer and redemption flows resolve recipients from stale saved data or similar names with no positive-match confirmation step, and completed transactions cannot be reversed.
examples: The customer argues Chase's system should never have allowed a points transfer into an account that had been closed for over 30 days.
Promotional points were deposited into a newly created frequent-flyer account he never authorized, which also had an incorrect surname, blocking his access to the points.

themes.root_cause: Fraud review policy equates successful authentication with authorization and gives no weight to contrary evidence such as police reports, video or coercion.

themes.name: Scam tricks the customer into sending the money
themes.problem_statement: Scammers posing as bank fraud staff, employers or partners convince the customer to wire or transfer their own money, and reimbursement is refused as customer-initiated.

examples: A caller posing as Chase's Fraud Department convinced the customer to send a transfer to 'reverse' a supposed unauthorized transaction, and the $750.00 never came back.

A $3,700.00 check from a dog-sitting job scam was deposited, and $3,200.00 was wired per the scammer's request before the customer grew suspicious; the branch said the funds probably cannot be recovered.

themes.name: Provisional fraud credit clawed back without explanation
themes.problem_statement: A temporary credit granted on a fraud claim is later reversed, in full or in part, without the evidence or the reasoning behind the reversal being shared.
themes.root_cause: The fraud re-investigation step reverses provisional credits on internal or merchant evidence that is never disclosed to the customer for rebuttal.
examples: After a phone and wallet theft abroad led to $870.00 in fraudulent ATM, purchase and transfer transactions, Chase issued a temporary credit but then withdrew it days later after review.
A fourth fraud dispute was credited in full, but a later re-investigation reversed it again as legitimate even though the customer had no access to the account being charged.

themes.name: Red flags and evidence of fraud are not acted on
themes.problem_statement: Fraud continues or claims are mishandled because freeze requests, staff warnings, prior reports and clear evidence that the customer was not responsible go unused.
themes.root_cause: Fraud operations do not reliably act on signals they already hold, such as alerts, escalations, submitted evidence and freeze requests, causing preventable losses.
examples: Chase cashed a forged $1200.00 check into the thief's own Chase account and will not refund the stolen money.
Fraudsters ran chargebacks and a fake mobile check deposit through the compromised checking account, and Chase is now charging the customer for the resulting balance.

themes.name: Identity thieves open accounts and loans in someone's name
themes.problem_statement: Fraudsters use a stolen identity to open deposit, loan or investment accounts, or to activate an unused card, unnoticed until money moves or credit is damaged.
themes.root_cause: Identity verification at account opening, loan origination and card activation does not adequately confirm the applicant, letting identity thieves through.
examples: A $64,000.00 auto finance account was opened without her knowledge or a contractual agreement, and she keeps receiving messages threatening to affect her credit.
A debit card the customer never activated was activated and used by someone else to place several orders, reported to police and the FBI.

themes.name: Fraud claim denied on an unrelated technicality
themes.problem_statement: A fraud claim is rejected under a rigid categorical rule about card age, merchant history, transaction type or who technically initiated it, rather than on the evidence.
themes.root_cause: Claim intake applies fixed eligibility rules that auto-deny whole categories of claims without any review of the specific evidence submitted.
examples: Multiple unauthorized transactions were posted to the checking account and the fraud dispute was closed as invalid because the card was too new to be considered fraud.
A $570.00 fraudulent gift card purchase claim was denied because Chase said the charge came from a merchant the customer had used before, despite no matching purchase found.

themes.name: One fraud incident refunded only in part
themes.problem_statement: Transactions from a single fraud incident are decided differently, some refunded and others denied, with no consistent explanation for the split.
themes.root_cause: Claims from one incident are adjudicated separately per transaction rather than as a single event, producing inconsistent outcomes for equally evidenced charges.
examples: Fraudulent charges of $1500.00 hit my Chase Business account and Chase refunded only $800.00, citing a 30-day policy for the rest.

Six $1900.00 transfers the customer never authorized went to a business using slightly different names each time; Chase reversed only two, leaving a $7600.00 loss after reversing its initial offer to credit all six.

themes.name: Fraudster logs into an existing account remotely
themes.problem_statement: A fraudster uses remote access, a phished password or a cloned phone number to get into an existing account and move money, undetected until after the loss.
themes.root_cause: Account-access monitoring does not reliably detect anomalous remote sessions, unauthorized logins or phished-credential use before the funds leave the account.
examples: A scam cloned my father's phone number to access a linked checking account through a number provided by Chase, and $13,000 was removed without consent.
A loan scammer gained remote access to the account and deposited a fake check via mobile deposit without permission, and Chase later insisted the check was genuinely the customer's.

themes.name: Obviously fraudulent check accepted despite red flags
themes.problem_statement: A forged, altered or mismatched check is accepted despite visible red flags such as a wrong payee name, mismatched address or missing endorsement, and the loss lands on the customer.
themes.root_cause: Check and mobile-deposit acceptance does not reliably screen endorsement, signature and payee-mismatch red flags before funds are made available.
examples: A bleached and fraudulently renamed rent check deposited without detection was promised reimbursement within 14 days, but the claim was later denied for a time lapse with no defined deadline ever given.
Chase allowed a mobile deposit of a $6200.00 US Treasury check into an account whose name, address and state did not match the check, with a missing or incorrect endorsement.

themes.name: Fraud loss charged to the victim, not the fraudster
themes.problem_statement: The fraud claim is denied and the customer is held responsible for the stolen money, blamed for not protecting the account, even when a bank error enabled the theft.
themes.root_cause: Fraud-claim review may default to account-holder liability for weak account protection without first testing whether a bank error, such as a card mailed to a wrong address, enabled the theft.
examples: Chase sent a replacement debit card to an address 15 miles away that wasn't the customer's, which was then used to withdraw $400.00 and $2,900.00, but the claim was denied for not taking adequate steps to protect the acc
Months of rent payments were reversed without the customer's authorization, money was sent to strangers through a payment app, and the bank held the customer liable, leaving the account negative.

themes.name: Fraud denied because customer couldn't prove innocence
themes.problem_statement: A fraud claim is denied or reversed because the customer cannot produce proof they did not make the charge (exact timestamps, merchant documentation), rather than the bank proving the charge was autho
themes.root_cause: Fraud-claim review places the burden of proof on the customer to disprove involvement instead of requiring the bank to establish that the customer actually authorized the transaction.
examples: After a phone, purse and wallet theft, $1,200.00 in fraudulent checking transactions were denied by Chase, which says the customer must find documentation to prove fraud.

themes.name: Stranger added as authorized user without owner's consent
themes.problem_statement: A stranger is added as an authorized user and issued a card without the account holder's consent, and the resulting fraudulent charges are not stopped or explained.
themes.root_cause: Authorized-user and card-issuance controls may not verify the existing account holder's consent, letting a fraudster add themselves to an established account.
examples: Chase added a stranger as an authorized user and mailed them a secondary card without the account owner's consent or two-factor verification, then would not disclose who or where the card was sent.
Someone was added as an authorized user without consent and charged thousands of dollars to the credit line before Chase refunded the money.

themes.name: Stolen reward points not restored after fraud is refunded
themes.problem_statement: Reward points fraudulently redeemed during a fraud incident are never credited back, even after the dollar charges from the same incident are refunded or the fraud is confirmed.
themes.root_cause: Fraud remediation reverses disputed dollar transactions but likely has no equivalent process for reinstating loyalty or reward points redeemed in the same incident.
examples: Reward points were used without authorization for a $62.00 purchase on an account that wasn't the customer's; the $62.00 was refunded quickly but the stolen points have not been returned.
Reward points from two long-held credit cards were redeemed for gift cards at the same time as other fraudulent transactions, but Chase concluded the customer benefited and took no further action.

themes.name: Identity-theft account stays on the credit report
themes.problem_statement: A credit account opened through identity theft keeps appearing on the customer's credit report, and disputes or blocking requests do not get it removed.
themes.root_cause: Credit-report dispute handling may not reliably investigate, block or delete tradelines the customer has documented as fraudulent with a police or identity-theft report.
examples: Fraudulent accounts and inquiries appearing on the credit report are requested to be deleted immediately.
A fraudulent JPMCB card account the customer never opened appears on the credit report, and the customer demands a wet-ink signed contract as validation within 14 days or the debt be deleted.

themes.name: Confirmed fraud account still reported and collected on
themes.problem_statement: An account opened through identity theft keeps being reported to credit bureaus and pursued for payment even after a police report, FTC report or FCRA 605B block request is filed.
themes.root_cause: Fraud resolution may not trigger the steps that stop bureau reporting and halt collections once an identity-theft report or 605B block request is on file.
examples: A fraudulent account opened through identity theft should be permanently removed from the credit report under FCRA Section 605B.
An account opened using compromised personal information continues to be reported even after an FTC Identity Theft Report was provided, which FCRA 605B requires to be blocked.
